beats.narration_text: Hey Claude — I just read Satwika's final brand portfolio for INFO 7375. Behavrix: a human risk intelligence platform that models employee behavioral archetypes mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, generating a vendor risk report in 90 seconds for two dollars. What does the work tell us?

props.command: I just read Satwika's final brand portfolio. Behavrix — human risk intelligence for security analysts, MITRE-mapped behavioral archetypes, 90-second reports. What does the work tell us?

beats.role_note: The brief — what was required and what was submitted.
beats.narration_text: Path B required a complete brand system for an AI tool startup. Satwika submitted 14 slides covering strategy, competitive analysis, visual identity, storytelling, and a live Streamlit tool. The origin story ties directly to a real co-op experience in cybersecurity — which is the right foundation.

props.heading: The Brief vs. The Delivery
props.body: All five Path B elements present. Origin story tied to real cybersecurity co-op. Live Streamlit tool publicly accessible. 14 slides, tight structure.

beats.role_note: Strength 1 — The competitive position is specific and defensible.
beats.narration_text: The competitive table compares Behavrix against KnowBe4, Prevalent, and Drata across six dimensions. The cost line is the most powerful: two dollars per report versus enterprise pricing. The structural impossibility of enterprise GRC vendors matching that price is a genuine unfair advantage claim, not just marketing language.

beats.role_note: Strength 2 — MITRE ATT&CK mapping is real product work.
beats.narration_text: Mapping the four behavioral archetypes — the Clicker, the Password Recycler, the Shadow IT User, the Over-Trusted Insider — directly to MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs is the strongest technical move in the submission. It turns a behavioral model into something a security analyst can cite in a report. That's a design decision that shows domain knowledge.

beats.narration_text: Four archetypes, four MITRE codes: T1566 for phishing clickers, T1078 for credential recyclers, T1072 for shadow IT, T1134 for over-trusted insiders. Each archetype has a name, a pattern, and a framework reference. This is exactly the specificity a security analyst needs to defend a finding to a board.

props.heading: MITRE archetype map
props.body: Four archetypes mapped to MITRE codes: T1566 Clicker, T1078 Password Recycler, T1072 Shadow IT, T1134 Over-Trusted Insider.

beats.role_note: Visual identity — palette and typography decisions.
beats.narration_text: The visual system uses Deep Navy, Teal, Blue, Frost, Soft Teal, and Amber — with Amber reserved for medium risk only. That functional color assignment is correct for a risk product. IBM Plex Sans for headings, Roboto for body, IBM Plex Mono for MITRE codes. No shields, no padlocks. That's a deliberate and right call.

beats.role_note: Brand voice and content — LinkedIn and Substack presence.
beats.narration_text: The LinkedIn post is stat-first and short — built for scroll. The Substack article provides long-form credibility. Both are live and public. That channel differentiation is the right choice: LinkedIn for awareness, Substack for depth. The two together reinforce the brand's transparency pillar.

props.heading: Channel Differentiation
props.body: LinkedIn stat-first for scroll, Substack long-form for depth. Both live. Both reinforce transparency — which is Behavrix's first brand pillar.

beats.role_note: Gap 1 — The 270-record dataset needs more transparent methodology.
beats.narration_text: The tool analyzes 270 records to generate a human risk score. That's stated as a fact but never explained. Where did the 270 records come from? How were the archetype classifications derived? For a product selling on transparency and data-attributed scoring, the data source is a gap that a CISO will ask about immediately.

props.heading: Transparency Gap in the Data
props.body: 270 records, but no methodology for how archetypes were derived. A CISO will ask. The brand's first pillar is transparency — the data source needs to be owned.

beats.role_note: Gap 2 — The pitch slide asks for 150K seed on slide 14 — too fast.
beats.narration_text: The final slide asks for 150,000 seed funding with 15 percent equity and an advisory board seat. For a student capstone, that's fine as a pitch exercise. But the financial projections — 10 paying customers in 90 days, 25K MRR in 12 months — aren't grounded in any customer discovery evidence. The pitch would be stronger without the investment ask or with one real customer conversation cited.

props.heading: Pitch Slide vs. Evidence
props.body: Investment ask and MRR projections appear without supporting customer discovery. Either cite one real conversation or remove the ask — unsupported projections undercut the credibility the brand builds everywhere else.

beats.role_note: Manim — 3 user test sessions vs. the enterprise CISO claim.
beats.narration_text: Three real user test sessions are cited. One of the personas is a CISO who reports to the board. The gap is scope: three tests, enterprise-level claims. The user testing section should either stay at proof-of-concept framing or expand — a quote from a real security practitioner, even a single one, would transform the credibility of this submission.

props.heading: 3 user tests vs. enterprise claim
props.body: Three user test sessions cited. One persona is a CISO reporting to a board. Gap: three tests support proof-of-concept framing, not enterprise validation.

beats.role_note: Live tool — what the Streamlit app delivers.
beats.narration_text: The live Streamlit tool takes an organization type from ten options, analyzes 270 records in approximately 90 seconds, and outputs a human risk score with behavioral personas and MITRE mapping. The cost is two-tenths of a cent per run. That's the right demo — fast, cheap, specific, and the result is something you can show a CISO.

props.heading: What the Tool Actually Does
props.body: Select org type, 90 seconds, $0.002 per run. Output: risk score, four behavioral personas, MITRE codes, board-ready language. The demo is the brand promise fulfilled.

beats.narration_text: Strong competitive positioning, real domain knowledge, MITRE mapping that holds up to scrutiny. The tool delivers on the brand promise. The gaps are in data transparency, user testing scope, and a pitch slide that overreaches the evidence. Fix those and the submission is genuinely compelling.

props.artifactHeading: Real domain knowledge and defensible competitive position — the tool fulfills the brand promise.
